reconcile.connective: Commentators read Christ's 'light' burden as inward rest amid real affliction, not a promise that discipleship escapes suffering or persecution.

discrepancy.empty_note: No individually named critic could be confirmed pressing this specific 'easy yoke' vs. persecution/chastisement pairing as a hard contradiction. Skeptic's Annotated Bible tags Matthew 11:28-30 only with an 'Absurdity' marker, not a contradiction, and does not cross-reference John 16:33 / 2 Timothy 3:12 / Hebrews 12:6,8 against it; this row instead traces to evilbible.com's uncredited web compilation, not a named critic. Even critical NT scholarship (Davies-Allison, Luz, per this row's own scholarship field) reads the 'easy yoke' as relative to the Mosaic/Pharisaic burden it replaces rather than an absolute claim of painlessness, which undercuts a sharply-pressed skeptical case.

excerpts.excerpt_text: [2.] The burden of Christ's cross is a light burden, very light: afflictions from Christ, which befall us as men; afflictions for Christ, which befall us as Christians; the latter are especially meant. This burden in itself is not joyous, but grievous; yet as it is Christ's, it is light. … Let this therefore reconcile us to the difficulties, and help us over the discouragements, we may meet with, both in doing work and suffering work; though we may lose for Christ, we shall not lose by him.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Henry explicitly concedes the 'light' burden is 'not joyous, but grievous' in itself — real affliction and 'suffering work' — yet calls it light because it is borne with and for Christ, directly bridging Matt 11:30's ease language with the persecution/suffering texts on the other pole.

excerpts.excerpt_text: For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light--Matchless paradox, even among the paradoxically couched maxims in which our Lord delights! That rest which the soul experiences when once safe under Christ's wing makes all yokes easy, all burdens light.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: JFB names 'easy yoke, light burden' a deliberate paradox resolved by the soul's inward rest under Christ, explaining how outwardly hard experience can still truthfully be called 'light' without denying the hardship exists.

excerpts.excerpt_text: May easily be borne. For his commandments are not grievous, for all that is born of God overcometh the world, 1 John 5:4.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: The Geneva annotators gloss 'easily borne' by cross-referencing 1 John 5:4's 'overcometh the world' — the same victory-over-tribulation theme John 16:33 invokes — tying the easy-yoke language to the very tribulation-overcoming framework the discrepancy claims it conflicts with.

pd_work.resource: John W. Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874), p. 179, entry "Christian yoke, easy. — Burdensome."
pd_work.author: John W. Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats this exact pairing verbatim under the heading 'Christian yoke, easy. Burdensome,' setting Matt 11:28,30 against John 16:33 and Heb 12:6,8, and answers that the yoke is 'easy' because Christianity 'is far less burdensome' than false religions and is 'congruous with man's reason, conscience, and all his nobler instincts,' while it is 'burdensome' because true religion 'comes in direct collision with the deep sinfulness of the human heart' and the Christian must 'pass through many a sore trial and conflict.'
